title: LA P2
text:
Suppose V is finite dimensional vector space and \(T: V \rightarrow V\) is a linear map such that \({v, T(v), ..., T^{(n-1)}(v)}\) is a basis for V. If \(S: V -> V\) is a linear transformation such that \(ST = TS\), prove that \(S(x) = a_0I + a_1T(x) + ... + a_nT^{(n-1)}(x)\) for some \(a_i\)






NoteSolution





Suppose \(S(v) = a_0 v + a_1 T(v) + ... + a_n T(v)^{(n-1)}\) we claim that the \(a_i\) satisfy \(S(x) = a_0 v + a_1 T(x) + ... + a_n T(x)^{(n-1)}\). Let \(P(x) = S(x) = a_0 v + a_1 T(x) + ... + a_n T(x)^{(n-1)}\). By definition of a_i, we have P(v) = S(v). Because ST = TS, we obtain that \(ST^k = T^kS\). Also because P is a polynomial of T, thus \(PT^k = T^KP\). Thus we have \(P(T^k(v)) = T^k(P(V)) = T^k(S(v)) = S(T^k(v))\). Because \({v, Tv, T^2v, ..., T^{(n-1)v}}\) is a basis for V and P and S have the same outputs, thus S = P.

title: LA3
text:
Suppose V is a vector space such that \(dim(V) >= 2\). If \(F\) is infinite prove that V can not be union of finitely many proper subspaces.






NoteSolution





Suppose for the sake of contradiction that V can be written as union of finitely many proper subspaces. Then V we can remove the subspaces that are subsets of each other and conclude that V can be writter as: \(V = U_1 \cup U_2 \cup ... \cup U_k\) where \(U_i \nsubseteq \bigcup_{j \neq i} U_j\) for all i, where \(U_i\) are proper subspaces of V. Choose \(u \in U_1\) s.t \(u \notin \bigcup_{i=2}^{k}U_i\). Because \(U_1\) is proper subspace of V, there exist some \(v \in V-U_1\). Consider the vectors \(u+tv\) where \(t \in F\). if \(t \neq 0\) then \(u+tv \notin U_1\). We claim that for all \(U_i, i>1\), at most one of the vectors \(u+tv\) are in \(U_i\). Suppose for the sake of contradiction that \(u+t_1v, u+t_2v \in U_i\). Then: \((t_1-t_2)v \in U_i \implies v \in U_i \implies u \in U_i\) which is a contradiction. Because there are finitely many \(u+tv\) in \(U_1 \cup U_2 \cup ... \cup U_k\) but the number of vectors in the form \(u+tv\) is infinite, thus there exists some \(u+t^*v \notin U_1 \cup U_2 \cup ... \cup U_k = V\) which is a contradiction

title: Linear Algebra — Midterm Exam
text:
Consider the vector space \(V=P_3(\mathbb{R})\), and let
\[
A=\{f\in V\mid f(0)f(1)=1\}.
\]
(a) Is \(A\) a subspace of \(V\)?
(b) Find the span of \(A\), i.e., \(\operatorname{span}(A)\).

title: Linear Algebra — Midterm Exam
text:
Question 2
Let \(F\) be a field and \(V\) a vector space over \(F\). Suppose that \(n\geq 3\) and that \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) are linearly independent vectors in \(V\).
Consider the following vectors:
\[
u_i=v_i+v_{i+1},\qquad 1\leq i<n,
\]
and
\[
u_n=v_n+v_1.
\]
(a) If \(F=\mathbb{R}\), prove that \(u_1,\ldots,u_n\) are linearly independent.
(b) Give an example of a field \(F\), a vector space \(V\) over \(F\), and linearly independent vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) such that \(u_1,\ldots,u_n\) are linearly dependent.

title: Linear Algebra — Midterm Exam
text:
Question 3
Consider the vector space
\[
V=\mathbb{F}_3^3
\]
and the following subset:
\[
W=\{(x,y,z)\in V\mid x+y+z=0\}.
\]
(a) Find a basis for \(W\).
(b) Determine the number of ordered triples
\[
(v_1,v_2,v_3)
\]
that form a basis for \(V\).
(c) Determine the number of two-dimensional subspaces of \(V\).

title: Linear Algebra — Midterm Exam
text:
Question 4
Suppose \(U\) and \(W\) are finite-dimensional subspaces of a vector space \(V\).
Prove that
\[
\dim(U+W)=\dim U+\dim W-\dim(U\cap W).
\]

title: Linear Algebra — Midterm Exam
text:
Question 5
Let
\[
G=\{g_1,\ldots,g_n\}
\]
be a basis for a vector space \(V\), where \(n\geq 2\).
Suppose that
\[
v=\sum_{k=1}^{n}a_kg_k,
\qquad
w=\sum_{k=1}^{n}b_kg_k,
\]
where \(v,w\) are linearly independent.
(a) Prove that there exist two distinct indices \(i,j\) such that
\[
(G\setminus\{g_i,g_j\})\cup\{v,w\}
\]
is a basis for \(V\).
(b) For two distinct indices \(i,j\), find a necessary and sufficient condition on the coefficients \(a_i,a_j,b_i,b_j\) such that
\[
(G\setminus\{g_i,g_j\})\cup\{v,w\}
\]
forms a basis for \(V\).
